content: The concentration of lead in air was reported as 85 mg per liter. However, a concentration of 0.15 mg per cubic meter was not specified. Zielhuis conducted a comprehensive review and analysis of data from various researchers regarding human absorption of lead, focusing on the relationships between blood lead levels, delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), and coproporphyrin. A blood lead concentration of 80 mg per liter is considered evidence of an unacceptable level of occupational lead exposure. Zielhuis did not examine the relationships between airborne lead concentrations and various biological indices of absorbed lead's effects. Kehoe identified a critical threshold for lead in blood, stating that a concentration of 0.08 mg of lead per 100 grams of whole blood is the level below which no cases of even mild lead poisoning have been observed. However, higher concentrations increase the likelihood of lead poisoning, though not all individuals with elevated levels will develop symptoms. The scientific consensus supports Kehoe's findings, particularly in adults. Nevertheless, even with the most accurate analytical methods, there is an inherent margin of error of approximately 10% in specific lead determinations. Environmental data presented in this section were selected to achieve two objectives: (1) to correlate measured environmental and biological lead levels with specific lead-utilizing industries, and (2) to link exposure levels to clinical manifestations of lead intoxication. In the context of leaded steel production, hazardous occupational lead exposures can occur. Ruhf reported that the highest atmospheric lead concentrations were observed during the steel pouring process, where lead is introduced. Elevated exposures were also noted in other processes, such as rolling mills, with concentrations reaching 20 mg per cubic meter. Ruhf further described control measures and manufacturing techniques that can effectively minimize lead exposure.
